                    ### Question
                    A 32-year-old man presents to his primary care physician complaining of pain accompanied by a feeling of heaviness in his scrotum. He is otherwise healthy except for a broken arm he obtained while skiing several years ago. Physical exam reveals an enlarged “bag of worms” upon palpation of the painful scrotal region. Shining a light over this area shows that the scrotum does not transilluminate. Which of the following statements is true about the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Equally common on both sides
opb. More common on left due to drainage into inferior vena cava
opc. More common on left due to drainage into renal vein
opd. More common on right due to drainage into inferior vena cava
ope. More common on right due to drainage into renal vein

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's symptoms of scrotal pain and heaviness, along with the physical exam finding of an enlarged 'bag of worms' that does not transilluminate, are indicative of a varicocele. Varicoceles are more common on the left side due to the anatomical drainage pattern where the left testicular vein drains into the left renal vein, which can lead to increased venous pressure. This is consistent with standard medical consensus. The retrieved evidence paths, while broad, support the understanding that palpation findings can indicate a varicocele. Therefore, the correct statement is that varicoceles are more common on the left due to drainage into the left renal vein, aligning with option 'opc'.
